content:
You have watched someone in the Core Group show up and serve, week after week. Emerging Leadership grows from people like that, and developing them is part of the Senior Pastor's work. An empty seat on the Launch Team is not the same thing as a missing leader.

This guide is for that first conversation. Name a specific contribution. Ask what they want to develop. Agree on a next conversation before you propose any role. A signal of steady attendance and serving can be the reason you ask. It is not a verdict.

---

## Why this talk comes before a role

Leaders for the launch should come from the Core Group, not from a last-minute search to fill a chart. [Key Leadership Roles Overview](/wiki/launch-team/leadership/key-leadership-roles-overview) already says to notice potential early, give small responsibilities, and watch for faithfulness. It also says not to appoint someone just because a vacancy is open. This article covers only the first talk. A small responsibility, if you ever offer one, belongs in a later conversation.

Explore before you ask. You are not recruiting them into a defined trial in this meeting. You are finding out whether the contribution you noticed is something they want to grow.

An open talk can leave someone unsure what you wanted. Close that gap in the room. Tell them what you noticed, tell them you are not offering a role today, and leave with a date. If they cannot repeat those three things, you were too vague.

| In this conversation | Not in this conversation |
| --- | --- |
| Name one contribution you saw | Offer a title, a trial, or a team |
| Ask what they want to develop | Decide they are called to a role |
| Set a date for the next talk | Fill an empty seat because it is empty |

<Callout type="important">
60 days of steady attendance and serving, both of them across the same stretch, can invite this conversation. Attendance alone does not. Serving alone does not. A shorter stretch does not. The signal asks whether you have considered more for this person. It never proves they are ready, and it never assigns a role. Character, doctrine, gifting, teachability, and relational maturity still take your judgment, in person.
</Callout>

---

## Start from a contribution you can name

Do not book this conversation because a role is empty. No assigned ministry roles means coverage needs attention. It does not mean emerging leaders are absent. Someone may already be serving faithfully and has not been asked what they want to grow in.

Look for a contribution you could put a date on. They stayed to reset the kids' room after the Vision Meeting and checked the sign-in list before they left. They learned two guests' names and wrote the follow-up themselves. "They have a great heart" will not hold up in the conversation.

If you cannot name the contribution, wait and watch. Thank them for the work when you see it. Do not dress that thank-you up as a leadership talk.

If you are not the Senior Pastor, take what you saw to the Senior Pastor before you imply any future responsibility. A side conversation that hints at a title creates a promise you cannot keep. That work sits with [The Senior Pastor Role](/wiki/launch-team/leadership/senior-pastor-role).

---

## Say what you saw, then let them answer

Ask for a short private conversation. Do not spring this in the Core Group meeting, and do not hold it where the setup team can hear. Tell them why you are asking, so they are not guessing on the way there.

You might say this. "I have watched you greet guests by name for several weeks, including the Sunday you walked a family to the kids' room and then came back to finish stacking chairs. I am not asking you to take a role. I want to tell you what I have seen, and I want to hear what you want to grow in."

Use "I see this in you" only when the next sentence is the example. If you cannot supply the example, drop the phrase. A compliment with no scene behind it is easy to shrug off, and it can sound like you are shopping for someone to plug a hole.

Then stop. Do not follow the observation with the role you hope they will take. That second sentence turns the talk into an appointment.

<Callout type="tip">
Write the contribution down before you meet, in one or two sentences a guest could verify. If the note is only an adjective, you are not ready for this conversation.
</Callout>

---

## Ask what they want to develop

Your questions are about their interest, not about your vacancy.

- Which part of that serving has felt most like you?
- What would you like to get better at?
- What would you rather not be asked to carry?
- Is there a person you already help that you want to keep helping?

Listen longer than you talk. Their answer may not match the open seat you had in mind. That is a useful result, not a failed meeting. After you part, write down their words. Do not write a score, and do not write a verdict.

If they ask whether you are offering children's ministry, worship, or anything else, answer directly. "No. I noticed your care with families. I do not know yet whether a role fits, and I will not decide that here." Then return to what they want to develop.

If they already want a role, thank them for saying so. Still do not appoint them, and do not invent a trial on the spot. Willingness is not a fit you have watched. The next conversation is where you look at a possible next step together.

---

## Set the next conversation before any role

Before you stand up, agree on the next talk. Name the day and the time. "We should stay in touch" is not an agreement. An unnamed follow-up is how exploring first delays a useful next step. A dated second conversation is that next step.

Say what the second conversation is for. You will come back to what they want to develop. You may then talk about a small responsibility, with support and a point to review it. You are not having that talk today. A larger role waits until faithfulness shows up in something smaller.

If their interest is groups, the apprentice path in [The Small Group Leader Role](/wiki/launch-team/leadership/small-group-leader-role) is also later. Do not hand them a group, a coach seat, or a title in this first talk.

Leave with this checklist done:

- [ ] You named one specific contribution, with a scene they would recognize.
- [ ] You asked what they want to develop, and you can repeat their answer.
- [ ] You said this is not a role offer and not a judgment of calling.
- [ ] You agreed on a day and time for the next conversation.
- [ ] You wrote down their words, not a fitness score.

<Callout type="warning">
A decline, a pause, or a different interest is a complete answer. Do not argue from the empty seat. Do not treat hesitation as a character problem. They may say no, and they may want time.
</Callout>

---

## Mistakes that turn notice into an appointment

"God is calling you to lead this ministry." You do not know that from attendance, serving, or one conversation. Do not put a calling in their mouth.

"We need a Worship Leader, and you came to mind." That is a vacancy talking. It skips what they want to develop.

"You have been here long enough, so you are ready." Time in the room is not readiness. The candidate signal exists so you will consider a conversation, not so you can skip judgment.

"The count says you are a leader now." Everyfield can hold a candidate signal from dated attendance and serving. It cannot judge calling, character, or fitness, and it does not certify anyone. The app does not have this conversation for you.

Praise in the moment is good. The same words in front of the Core Group pressure them to answer before they have thought.

---

## Keep the judgment with a person

After the talk, compare what they said with what you have seen. If the two do not match, believe the slower evidence. A confident answer over coffee is not faithfulness you can watch.

Do not record this conversation as a fitness result or a role assignment. Later judgments stay human and dated. A model must not infer fitness from your notes. Missing notes are your next step, not a hidden conclusion. Everyfield does not certify the person, gate a role on this talk, or coach the conversation in the app.

If the second conversation never gets booked, the first one was unfinished. Send the reminder yourself. Emerging Leadership does not appear because a chart has blanks. It appears when someone notices a real contribution and learns what that person wants to carry. How that factor sits with the others is in [8 Critical Success Factors Overview](/wiki/frameworks/8-critical-success-factors-overview).

<Callout type="scripture">
*"Therefore, comfort one another and build up one another, just as you also are doing."* — 1 Thessalonians 5:11 (LSB)
</Callout>

title: Having an "I See in You" Conversation

sources.claim: The conversation is for building the person up, which is why the article quotes 1 Thessalonians 5:11 rather than treating the talk as an appointment.
sources.publisher: Legacy Standard Bible, The Lockman Foundation
sources.quote: Therefore, comfort one another and build up one another, just as you also are doing.

claim_check.notes: Owner review by Sebastian; no model review per his 2026-10-26 instruction.

rulings: Bryan ruled R1 = Option A: "Explore before asking" (2026-10-26 1:31 PM ET).

Wording: kept the backlog title Having an "I See in You" Conversation so the named practice stays findable. The body teaches explore-before-asking and does not teach a defined trial in the first conversation.
Wording: sort_order 12, after the leadership role articles at sort_order 1-11 in seed.json, because this is a conversation practice rather than a role page.

Wording: a later small responsibility remains consistent with launch-team/leadership/key-leadership-roles-overview and the small-group apprentice path, and is deferred to a second dated conversation. This article does not script that ask.

Wording: the 60-day candidate signal is stated as Everyfield methodology from REQ-TEAM-017 and Bryan C07, not as an external research finding. It is omitted from draft.sources because those records have no fetched public URL and exact quote.

Wording: Hernandez, Churches Plant Churches, and Spratt and Medders, Discerning a Call to Ministry, are background only. They are not cited in the article or in draft.sources, and no text was copied from them.
Wording: if the reader is not the Senior Pastor, they take the observation to the Senior Pastor before implying a future responsibility.

Wording: sentence-case headings. Gender-neutral wording. Four C's and assessment colors are not named in the body. The software limit is stated as no judgment of calling, character, or fitness, and no model inference of fitness from notes.
